title: Accommodation matters, for foundation year students too
summary: Difficulties in securing and affording accommodation affect all new students. But, as Wendy Ashall's research demonstrates, it hits particularly hard for foundation year students
full_text:
The Office for Students published its Explorations: Student Experiences of Accommodation report in June 2026.

It is the most comprehensive, student-centred evidence base on accommodation the regulator has produced to date.

Based on a survey of 1,293 first-year students and qualitative research with a further 21 participants, it paints an important picture of how accommodation shapes students’ lives, choices, and wellbeing.

It is rigorous, timely, and welcome. It also has a significant blind spot, one that my doctoral research on Foundation Year (FY) students reveals, and one with consequences that reach far beyond any single student cohort.

What the OfS got right

The report confirms what many of us in higher education have long argued: accommodation is not a peripheral concern. It is central to whether students feel they belong, whether they succeed academically, and whether they can afford to stay. Several findings stand out.

Information inequality in accommodation decision-making is real and consequential. Students entering via UCAS Extra, Clearing, or as their insurance choice, reported reduced options, constrained choices, and lower satisfaction, not because of their own failings, but because the timing of the admissions system left them with whatever accommodation remained. The OfS rightly identifies this as a problem. So does my research, and not only in relation to accommodation.

On-campus, provider-maintained accommodation consistently outperforms private alternatives across almost every metric in the report: satisfaction, social integration, sense of belonging, academic impact, and issue resolution. Students in university accommodation were more likely to feel their living situation positively affected their academic performance (71 per cent vs. 49 per cent for those in private student accommodation). This matters for how institutions think about widening participation, and it is consistent with the findings of my own research.

The financial picture is stark. 89 per cent of students had taken additional steps to cover accommodation costs, borrowing from family, working extra hours, or reducing energy use. 15 per cent found it genuinely difficult to meet costs. The report also finds that maintenance loans routinely fall short of actual rents. These are not individual financial management failures: they are systemic affordability pressures, and the OfS is right to document them.

Finally, the finding that 86 per cent of students said accommodation costs influenced their choice of where to study deserves serious regulatory attention. Student “choice” in the HE market cannot be meaningfully exercised if a foundational practical concern (where to live) is experienced as a constraint rather than an active decision.

Extending our understanding

Foundation Year courses represent an important and growing route into higher education. They enable students, often those who narrowly missed entry requirements, or who applied late in the cycle, to enter university at a high-tariff institution, develop academic skills and confidence, and progress to an undergraduate degree. The Foundation Year Network has extensively documented their contribution to widening participation. But the structural conditions under which many FY students are recruited (though this varies by provider) create specific and compounding disadvantages, disadvantages that the OfS accommodation report inadvertently illuminates.

My doctoral research examined FY students’ experiences at a high-tariff English university, using a mixed-methods design: a group-administered survey of 119 students, analysis of their administrative data, and 21 in-depth interviews. I explored how students come to be enrolled in Foundation Year courses and what their subsequent experiences are like.

The OfS and I are looking at different cohorts and operating at different levels. But the overlaps are striking, and the divergences instructive.

On information and decision-making: both studies show that students rely on university services and informal networks for information, and that those entering late in the admissions cycle, whether via FY changed offers, UCAS Extra, or Clearing, face compounded disadvantages. The OfS documents this at the point of accommodation search. My research shows it more fundamentally at the point of late course acceptance.

On belonging and social integration: the OfS finds that accommodation is central to friendship formation, sense of belonging, and positive academic outcomes, with 75 per cent of students reporting accommodation had a positive impact on their social lives. My research independently confirms this but adds that for FY students, most of whom are recruited late in the application cycle, on-campus accommodation was both especially important and especially hard to access.

Students who arrived after A-level results were confirmed frequently found that on-campus places had already been allocated to students who had held offers since January. Being housed off campus left them feeling disconnected from peer networks, support services, and the developing student community. There is every reason to think the same applies to students entering via UCAS Extra or Clearing more broadly.

On financial pressures: the OfS documents widespread financial strain. My research situates this within a particularly acute structural problem for FY students: they accrue four years of non-cancellable tuition fee debt rather than three, often combined with significant living costs, yet frequently did not fully understand this financial commitment at the point of accepting their offer. One participant told me she had not thought about the fees until she arrived: “When I got here, I was like, oh, wow, that’s actually four years of debt.” This was not an unusual finding in my data.

Where the report falls short

The OfS report’s core limitation is not methodological; it is one of scope. The study focuses on accommodation choice as a decision students make. But for students recruited late in the admissions cycle, the more fundamental problem is that they were never meaningfully able to choose at all.

70 per cent of survey respondents in my study entered the Foundation Year via a “change of offer at confirmation”. They were redirected after their A-level results, in the final weeks of August, after the main admissions cycle had closed. These students did not choose the Foundation Year in any meaningful sense.

Many had applied for undergraduate courses, missed subject-specific grade requirements, and were offered a FY place by their first-choice university as an alternative, often within days of results release. They accepted because the alternative was Clearing, because they wanted to attend that university, and because they had limited information about what a Foundation Year was, what it would cost, or how it would affect their access to on-campus accommodation and social integration.

The same logic applies, with appropriate variation, to all students entering via UCAS Extra or Clearing into undergraduate courses. The time pressure, the information deficit, the lack of independent guidance: these are structural features of a pre-qualification admissions system that has not been meaningfully reformed in decades, and their downstream consequences, including in accommodation, are precisely what the OfS report is documenting. My FY data makes this visible in sharp relief. But the pattern is not unique to FY students. It is a late-cycle phenomenon.

The OfS itself has acknowledged the unreformed UCAS system as a concern. The accommodation report demonstrates the downstream consequences of information inequality at scale. But it does not, and cannot, address the admissions-level mechanisms producing it.

The students most likely to enter higher education via these late-cycle routes are disproportionately those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, first-generation students, and those from minoritised ethnic communities. These are also the students most dependent on on-campus accommodation for social integration, and least likely to have family networks who can help them navigate unfamiliar systems. The OfS report confirms that parental HE experience predicts better outcomes across almost every accommodation metric it measures. My research shows the same pattern operating at the point of admissions. This is not coincidence: it is the same structural inequality, encountered twice.

Late-cycle recruitment and the stakes ahead

The context in which these findings land matters. The UK HE sector is entering a period of significant demographic and financial pressure. Declining domestic applicant numbers in some subject areas, alongside ongoing constraints on international recruitment, are pushing institutions to recruit further into the admissions cycle, holding offers longer, expanding Clearing activity, and in some cases growing FY provision specifically to manage the risk of late-stage shortfalls.

This means more students will be recruited late in the cycle, not fewer. The structural problems my research identifies in FY admissions (time pressure, information deficits, constrained accommodation access, limited independent guidance) are not niche concerns. They are a preview of what late-cycle recruitment produces at scale, under growing institutional pressure to fill places.

If widening participation is a genuine regulatory priority, the conditions under which late-cycle students are recruited cannot remain unexamined. The OfS accommodation report documents the symptoms. My research identifies the mechanism. Both point to the same conclusion: the admissions system itself must be in scope.

What this means

The OfS accommodation report is a valuable contribution to the evidence base, and I hope it shapes regulatory action. But if the regulator is serious about equality of opportunity in student accommodation, it needs to look beyond the accommodation system itself.

Three things follow from placing this report alongside research on FY and other late-cycle entrants:

Universities should be required to reserve on-campus accommodation for students recruited late in the admissions cycle, including FY students who receive changed offers at confirmation, and those entering via UCAS Extra or Clearing. The evidence from both the OfS report and my own research is unambiguous: on-campus living supports belonging, integration, and academic engagement. Students who need it most are currently least likely to access it.

The forthcoming DfE review of HE admissions must address late-cycle recruitment specifically. Foundation Year courses provide an excellent alternative route into higher education, but students should not be accepting course offers, whether for FY or undergraduate programmes, under conditions of acute time pressure and inadequate information. Independent guidance at the point of confirmation and Clearing must be strengthened, for all students, not just those entering FY routes.

The National Student Survey should be extended to cover Foundation Year courses. The OfS cannot regulate what it cannot measure. FY students, a growing population now numbering in the tens of thousands, remain entirely outside the NSS framework. This is a regulatory gap the OfS is well-placed to close. Until it is closed, the sector cannot have a full picture of how late-cycle recruitment shapes student experience.

The OfS accommodation report shows that where students live shapes who they become at university. My research shows that for Foundation Year students, and, I would argue, for all students recruited late in the application cycle, the conditions determining that are set not by accommodation policy, but by admissions practice.

The two are not separate problems. They are the same problem, encountered at different points in the same journey. Both need to change.

title: Year of after-school care now costs £2,800 a child in parts of UK
summary:
Bills have jumped 42% in England over the past 10 years – and that excludes the cost of breakfast clubs and extracurricular activities

Parents of primary schoolchildren in England will pay 42% more for after-school childcare this year than they did 10 years ago, with annual bills now exceeding more than £2,800 a child in some parts of the UK.

A Guardian analysis of data collected by the children’s charity Coram has revealed that the annual cost of after-school care for children aged 5 to 11 in England has risen by 5% over the past year to £2,636.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Parents of primary schoolchildren in England will pay 42% more for after-school childcare this year than they did 10 years ago, with annual bills now exceeding more than £2,800 a child in some parts of the UK.

A Guardian analysis of data collected by the children’s charity Coram has revealed that the annual cost of after-school care for children aged 5 to 11 in England has risen by 5% over the past year to £2,636.

In Scotland the cost is even higher at £2,701, while in Wales prices have risen by 64% in the past 10 years and by 8% in the past year to £2,824.

Parents also typically pay £191 per child a week for childcare during the school holidays, Coram found, adding more than £1,700 to the total annual childcare bill.

These costs, which do not include breakfast clubs before school starts, are in addition to the price of extracurricular activities such as swimming and music lessons, sports clubs and dance classes.

Such activities now typically cost £700 a year and add up to £9,100 over a child’s time in school, research by Nationwide revealed today.

Parents also spend an average of £381 each year on school uniform and sports kit – including £43 on shoes, £37 on blazers and £29 on tracksuits – as well as £116 a year on school trips, Nationwide found.

“It’s never-ending, really, isn’t it, for parents?” said Lydia Hodges, the head of Coram Family and Childcare. “[When a child is at nursery], a lot of parents hear: ‘Oh it will be better when they go to school.’ But actually, once you factor in paying for after-school childcare and holiday childcare, it’s still a pretty big bill every month.”

The impact of these costs can be far-reaching, she said. “It’s very stressful, I think, for a lot of parents, and it’s something that they have to take into account in their budget when they’re thinking about: ‘Is it worthwhile working? Does work pay? How many children can we have?’”

Nearly half (49%) of the 2,002 UK parents and guardians surveyed by Nationwide said they are stressed about the cost of their children going back to school this September, and one in four are delaying non-essential purchases.

Between 2016 and 2026, latest figures from the Office for National Statistics show average weekly earnings rose by 51% to £700, although once these figures are adjusted for inflation, the statistics show average wages grew by only 7.5% in real terms. According to the Resolution Foundation, wages in the private sector this summer are barely keeping pace with price rises, while unemployment continues to hover at about 5%.

Anna*, a civil servant who has three children under the age of seven, said she and her husband take turns working from home to avoid paying for after-school childcare. “When you’ve got two school-age kids, it quickly comes to the point where you’re asking: what’s the point in working full-time really? So we manage by picking them up and bringing them home.”

As a result, she and her husband are constantly under pressure to juggle their working days around their children’s needs and activities. “Every week, we always have to have a discussion and a negotiation about who goes into the office.”

This year, she estimates she will spend – on each child – about £250 on their school uniform and shoes, even though she buys branded clothes second-hand through PTA uniform sales.

Other back-to-school items she needs to buy this year, such as backpacks and lunchboxes, can easily add up to £70 a child, she has discovered, putting her off making the purchases. “I haven’t pulled the trigger yet, because I got a bit of sticker shock.”

The couple are high earners but, after a summer of childcare costs and a cheap camping holiday, their bank account is almost empty. “We’re not frivolous spenders, so I can only imagine that for the vast majority of people, it’s impossible.”

Other parents have discovered they are expected to buy costly one-off equipment for their children to use at secondary school this year, such as expensive tablets and hi-tech calculators.

One parent, who wished to remain anonymous, contacted the Guardian about having to buy a tablet for their daughter to use at her “proudly smartphone-free school”, as well as a calculator “labelled so specifically that the cheapest one on the internet was over £25”.

“It’s bloody bonkers!” they wrote. “I am a teacher, and I have a kid starting year 7 [secondary school] in September. We’ve not had a holiday this summer, instead we’re kitting her out for secondary. I know sacrificing a holiday isn’t something lots of people are able to do – I know we’re among the lucky ones to be able to sacrifice a holiday instead of eating, or rent, or something else entirely more fundamental.”

The costs of sending her three young children back to school is something Ivana Poku, who runs the parenting blog mumsjourney.com, has also become increasingly aware of. “Having three children isn’t necessarily more expensive when they’re very young, but the costs seem to increase as they grow. School trips, activities, uniforms, shoes, sports equipment, lunches and all the other little things quickly add up – and when you have three children, you’re paying for everything three times,” she said. “I can completely understand why finances can influence how many children couples decide to have.”

*Anna did not wish to give her surname

title: Faculty Quit as Texas A&M Victoria Requires Them On Campus 5 Days a Week
summary:
Faculty Quit as Texas A&M Victoria Requires Them On Campus 5 Days a Week
Emma Whitford Tue, 08/25/2026 - 03:00 AM

The new policy, announced in June, is a response to a Texas law restricting remote work for public university faculty. The Texas AAUP says it has prompted chaos and tears.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
A number of faculty members at Texas A&M University–Victoria have quit after the university announced in late June that full-time faculty are required to be on campus for eight hours a day, five days per week this fall. As a result, multiple classes have been canceled and some departments are nearly empty, said Teresa Klein, president of the Texas chapter of the American Association of University Professors.

“It’s just chaos there,” said Klein, who teaches psychology at Del Mar College. “We’re hearing tears. There’s one woman who just had a baby who quit because she said, ‘I just can’t do this. I can’t be away from my child.’ We have people who are taking care of elderly relatives, and there’s just no way they can do that and be on the road for four hours a day.”

Nearly three-quarters—72 percent—of Texas A&M–Victoria faculty have addresses in the Houston area, which is about a two-hour drive from the Victoria campus. Others live as far away as San Antonio, Klein wrote in a blog post.

According to a June 26 email from the provost, which Klein read to Inside Higher Ed, “faculty are expected to have day-to-day physical presence on campus for in-person interaction with students, administration, other employees and the community,” and “to be on campus 5 days a week and maintain a 40-hour workweek.” Failure to comply “may subject an individual to discipline, up to and including termination.”

Texas A&M–Victoria officials did not answer Inside Higher Ed’s questions about the policy, but said in an emailed statement Monday that “flexibility is not an exemption from accountability.”

“Texas A&M University-Victoria is beginning a new chapter, but the standard is already clear. The Texas A&M University System holds its faculty and employees to high expectations, and A&M-Victoria will rise to meet them,” the statement read. “The university has communicated with faculty for more than a year about teaching loads and the importance of maintaining a meaningful campus presence. These expectations are consistent with Senate Bill 2615, other applicable state law and A&M System policy. This is ultimately about students. A&M-Victoria is welcoming a freshman class 23 percent larger than last year’s. Those students should find an active, vibrant campus and educators who are dedicated to their profession, engaged with their colleagues and invested in student success.”

Texas Senate Bill 2615 took effect in September 2025 and was authored by then senator, now Texas Tech University System Chancellor Brandon Creighton. The bill restricts telework for public higher education faculty members, but does not specifically require they spend 40 hours per week on campus. As of Monday, no other Texas A&M campuses appear to have implemented a similar rule.

In a letter to Texas A&M–Victoria officials, Klein said the rule misapplies the law.

“The bill’s original intent was to encourage a ‘reset’ after COVID, encouraging faculty to return to an on-campus presence following the pandemic, which had necessitated most faculty to work remotely. It is clear the bill’s original intent has now been sufficiently fulfilled,” she wrote. “Its continued application serves only to restrict faculty research, curricular and teaching productivity, innovation and optimal service to the students and taxpayers, while placing unreasonable, undue hardship and disparate effects on the personal and professional lives of faculty and their families.”

In the June email, the provost’s office told faculty members they would need to submit written permission to work remotely at least two weeks before the semester, which started on Aug. 24. Faculty were also asked to sign a form confirming their “understanding and commitment” to the policy by July 15.

Klein told Inside Higher Ed that AAUP members said as many as half of Texas A&M–Victoria’s full-time faculty have resigned, including the entire counselor education department. As of Monday evening, the Texas AAUP was still working to confirm exact numbers.

Texas A&M–Victoria has reached out to employees at Del Mar College, a community college in Corpus Christi, to recruit professors on short notice, Klein said. The Del Mar social sciences department’s administrative assistant received an email from someone at Texas A&M–Victoria stating they were “in a bit of a bind” and asking if anyone could teach a U.S. government class on Tuesdays and Thursdays, according to Klein.

There’s a lot of confusion on the Victoria campus, Klein said. Faculty members in different departments are getting different information—for example, one Texas AAUP member told Klein their department instructed them to check in at 8 a.m. and check out at 5 p.m. every weekday. Other professors were told by Texas A&M–Victoria officials that “if they can’t handle the new rules, they should just quit,” she said.

“The timing of the impromptu mandate has left many faculty scrambling to rearrange their schedules to accommodate, negatively affecting their professional and personal lives and having a possible disproportional, discriminatory and disparate negative effect on female faculty and those with long commutes to campus,” Klein wrote in her letter to Texas A&M–Victoria officials. “We have already seen multiple outstanding faculty … be ‘constructively terminated’—i.e., they had no choice but to ‘terminate themselves’ through resignation because they could not possibly or reasonably comply with this spur-of-the-moment edict.”

title: 5 Ways Colleges Are Reshaping STEM Education
summary:
5 Ways Colleges Are Reshaping STEM Education
Joshua.Bay Tue, 08/25/2026 - 03:00 AM

Colleges are redesigning gateway courses, expanding hands-on learning and creating new career paths to help more students succeed in STEM.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Getting more students into science, technology, engineering and mathematics has long been a higher education priority, but access alone doesn’t guarantee success.

Recent efforts show colleges rethinking how they support students across the STEM pathway—from redesigning gateway math courses and expanding hands-on learning to strengthening career preparation and creating new avenues into technology careers.

Here are five approaches institutions are taking to help students succeed in STEM as advances in technology and a changing workforce reshape what they need from higher education.

Make calculus less of a bottleneck.

Calculus has long been one of the biggest hurdles for students pursuing a STEM degree, with success in Calculus I often determining whether they continue in their field—or switch to something else.

To reduce that barrier, the nonprofit Every Learner Everywhere recently launched the Courseware Lighthouse Implementation Program, an initiative that brings together 12 public colleges and universities to redesign how Calculus I and II are taught.

Rather than introduce a new technology tool into individual classrooms, the initiative works with entire mathematics departments to rethink course design, strengthen faculty collaboration and use student performance data to refine instruction over time. The program follows a six-phase framework that guides departments through planning, implementation and ongoing evaluation, with the goal of improving student success in gateway math courses and helping more students persist in STEM majors.

Laura DaVinci, senior director of Every Learner Everywhere, said improving student outcomes in calculus involves more than adopting new technology; it requires rethinking how institutions support students and faculty throughout gateway math courses.

“It has to do a lot with the students’ perception that calculus is difficult,” DaVinci said. “When they go in with that anxiety and that, ‘Oh no, I know for a fact that only two-thirds of students ever pass calculus,’ it’s really daunting to go in wondering, ‘Am I going to be the student that fails?’”

Connect calculus to real-world engineering.

First offered at the University of Michigan in 2024, ROB 201: Calculus for the Modern Engineer was designed to more closely connect calculus with the work students will encounter as engineers, combining elements of Calculus I and II and differential equations with programming and robotics applications.

Jessy Grizzle, a professor of robotics at Michigan who developed the course, said the idea grew in part from years of hearing students describe a disconnect between the math they were learning and how they expected to use it as engineers.

Rather than beginning with differentiation—as traditional calculus courses typically do—students start with integration, using, for example, real data to calculate a drone’s trajectory from its acceleration. The course also pairs traditional pencil-and-paper calculus exercises that have exact solutions with messier, real-world problems that students rely on computer programming to solve.

Students learn to code in Julia, allowing them to use computation when a neat solution isn’t possible. Grizzle said the approach exposes students earlier to the kinds of challenges they will encounter as engineers, where data can be noisy and solutions less straightforward.

“I kept hearing from students that they felt beat down in the math department and unmotivated by just learning abstract concepts without them being tied to applications,” Grizzle said. “People become engineers because they want to create devices that we all hope improve the world.”

“So when the math seems completely divorced from that, there’s a segment of students who are flat out turned off by that,” he added. “They really need it tied to something more substantial, more concrete.”

Prepare computer science students for a changing field.

After a decade-long computer science boom, the City University of New York is confronting questions about whether it has enough instructional capacity—and the right expertise—to prepare students for a rapidly changing technology workforce.

A recent report from the Center for an Urban Future found that computer science enrollment at CUNY surged by 146 percent from 2014 to 2024, even as overall university enrollment declined. Faculty growth failed to keep pace with that expansion, however, creating potential bottlenecks for students trying to build careers in technology.

Those challenges arise as the technology sector itself is shifting. Numbers of entry-level tech jobs in New York City have fallen by 49 percent since 2022, while AI is changing the skills employers expect from new graduates. CUNY computer science enrollment also fell 15 percent between 2024 and 2025, from 10,330 to 8,819 students.

Eli Dvorkin, editorial and policy director at the Center for an Urban Future, said the combination of CUNY’s decade of enrollment growth and the fast-evolving tech economy has increased pressure to ensure that students have access to faculty with the capacity and expertise to prepare them for the workforce.

“Just a few years ago, a computer science degree alone could take a student pretty far,” Dvorkin said. “But in today’s much tougher entry-level job market, students need more applied skills, exposure to AI in context, real-world projects, industry connections and faculty who have the insights to help them connect to careers and enough time to mentor them.”

“That all raises the stakes enormously for getting the faculty piece right when it comes to computer science education,” he added.

Make AI learning more accessible.

This spring Santa Clara University launched AI Kitchen, a weekly workshop where students, faculty, staff and Silicon Valley professionals gather to experiment with emerging artificial intelligence tools.

Every Friday, about 50 participants meet for a nearly four-hour session to test new AI tools and explore how they’re used across fields ranging from medicine and marketing to education and real estate.

Kai Lukoff, assistant professor of computer science and engineering at Santa Clara, said the “AI Kitchen” name was chosen intentionally to signal a space that is more familiar, communal and creative than one associated with stereotypical tech culture.

To reinforce that accessibility, every session is intentionally kept “code-light,” allowing an anthropology major, a computer science student and a curious staff member to participate in the same hands-on exercises.

“What I wanted to start with AI Kitchen is not just a course about AI literacy, but what one might call AI fluency,” Lukoff said. “So not just having an understanding of the tools, but also hands-on ability to work with these tools, explore their strengths and weaknesses, and engage in real-world projects that apply them.”

Open new pathways into tech careers.

Marymount University’s From Caregiver to Breadwinner program is based on the premise that caregiving develops skills employers value but often overlook. The private Catholic university in Northern Virginia launched the workforce initiative in 2024 to help unpaid family caregivers transition into careers in information technology.

Through the no-cost, 12-week program, participants receive training in IT and artificial intelligence fundamentals, prepare for industry-recognized certifications, including CompTIA Tech+, and receive mentorship, career coaching and job-placement support. Established by the university’s Center for the Innovative Workforce, the program has served more than 140 participants so far.

Diane Murphy, director of the Center for the Innovative Workforce, said the idea emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic, when caregiving responsibilities pushed many people—particularly women—out of the workforce. As technology reshaped the job market and employers sought new digital skills, many caregivers faced challenges returning to work.

“We felt this was a needy population that nobody was really paying too much attention to,” Murphy said. “But if we’ve got a tech workforce crunch, they are people who already have good skills, particularly customer service skills, which are a little low in IT help desk work.”

“If we could take their existing skills and package them with some technology training, we could get them to reinvent themselves into the tech workforce,” she added.

title: FIU Violated Student Free Speech Rights, Judge Rules
summary:
FIU Violated Student Free Speech Rights, Judge Rules
kathryn.palmer… Tue, 08/25/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
A federal judge sided with student protesters who claimed Florida International University violated their First Amendment rights when it punished them for violating a policy that bans “expressive activities” inside campus buildings.

On Sunday, U.S. Southern District of Florida Judge Jacqueline Becerra ordered the Miami-based university to halt enforcement of the policy and temporarily blocked disciplinary actions against the students, court records show. It’s not yet clear if FIU will appeal the decision, though university officials have previously maintained that the policy is compliant with the First Amendment and Florida laws.

“FIU applies its rules prohibiting protests and demonstrations in university buildings consistently, regardless of viewpoint. This ensures that classes, research, and academic spaces can function without interference or disruption,” FIU spokesperson Madeline Baro told WLRN earlier this year. “The University allows protests and demonstrations in outdoor areas, giving people a meaningful way to share their views, just not inside university lecture halls, labs, offices, or residence halls.”

The ruling comes just two weeks after the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida filed a lawsuit on behalf of a group of seven student protesters who were punished for protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In March, the students—who are part of a group called ICEBreakers—wore shirts that read “ICE OFF FIU” while standing in silence for a few minutes during an on-campus event where FIU President Jeanette Nuñez was hosting a talk with former Major League Baseball player Alex Rodriguez.

According to the ACLU, the students were specifically protesting a university contract that allows campus police to conduct federal immigration enforcement.

Although students left the event in silence, a few months later FIU issued a written reprimand stating that the protest violated a campus policy against “expressive activities” taking place indoors.

According to local media reports, the university asked each student to record a two-minute video explaining “what is expected … related to indoor and outdoor areas, and how you will apply what you have learned moving forward.”

Some of the students said making such a video would force them to express opinions they don’t agree with and followed up with legal action. Per the judge’s ruling Sunday, the university should have never punished them to begin with.

“In short, when all is said and done, and for at least 60 years, the standard has been the same: student speech cannot be curtailed unless it materially disrupts the educational mission or involves substantial disorder or invasion of the rights of others,” Judge Becerra wrote in the preliminary injunction. “Based on the evidence submitted to date, it does not appear that any Plaintiff, or anyone else wearing an ‘ICE OFF FIU’ T-shirt, spoke or did anything other than sit, stand, and walk.”

title: Back to school: How to save on uniform costs
summary: From baby banks to supermarket deals, there are many ways parents can ease the back-to-school burden.
full_text:
Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.

Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.

And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.

New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.

From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.

Save the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.

The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents.

"Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.

Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.

In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops.

During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.

Parents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.

In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.

Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.

Hannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.

Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year.

"So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.

You may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.

These can be worth up to £200 per child.

Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.

Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor.

"Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal... it should be something positive," she said.

title: Cost of being parentless: Odisha rights panel orders probe into wrong parents’ names in certificates
summary: A parentless student finds difficulties in his academic journey and life as different imaginary parents’ names were recorded by child care institutes (orphanages). The mismatch deprives him of government assistance
full_text:
What is harder in life—being parentless or having different names recorded as parents in official documents? Praveen (name changed), a parentless boy from Odisha, has learnt the answer the hard way.

Raised in childcare institutions, Praveen fought against the odds to make his way to Gangadhar Meher University, Sambalpur, one of Odisha’s premier higher education institutions.

But discrepancies in the names of his parents recorded in his certificates and Aadhaar card have deprived him of government assistance, casting a shadow over both his identity and education.

Taking note of his ordeal, the Odisha Human Rights Commission (OHRC) has directed the Sundargarh district administration to probe how the discrepancies arose and explore remedial measures to correct his records.

“I had no idea how I landed in an orphanage or who my parents were—the uncertainty is an ordeal every parentless child lives with. But my life was thrown into turmoil when I found imaginary parents’ names in my certificates and Aadhaar card. The orphanages also showed little urgency in correcting the records, leaving me in all sorts of trouble,” said Praveen, who is pursuing his graduation at Gangadhar Meher University, Sambalpur.

When Praveen was five, someone left him at the gate of Sarbabhoutik Shishu Seba Ashram in Rourkela. The childcare institution was closed in 2012 for reasons that remain unclear, following which he was shifted to Rourkela Sishu Bhavan.

“At Sishu Bhavan, the names Munna Ekka and Kan Ekka were recorded as my father and mother. But when my Aadhaar card was made, P. K. Senapati, the superintendent of the institution, was recorded as my father. My ordeal began there,” Praveen recalled.

He alleged that the discrepancies between his certificates and Aadhaar card deprived him of government assistance meant for orphans and persons with disabilities. Praveen has a hearing disability.

After matriculation, he was denied admission when he sought to pursue Plus Two at Sundargarh Government College. The intervention of the Sundargarh district collector eventually resolved the issue.

“Without government assistance, I had to take tuition classes and work as a newspaper hawker to meet my expenses and survive,” he said.

Praveen said he repeatedly approached the authorities, drawing attention to the discrepancies in his records, but no corrective action was taken.

“When I tried to correct my Aadhaar card myself, executives at common service centres asked me for my date of birth, residence certificate and parents’ details—documents I simply did not have. I fear these discrepancies will ruin my career and my life,” he said.

During an awareness programme at the university in the third week of August, an Odisha Human Rights Commission (OHRC) team heard Praveen’s account. He submitted a written account of his ordeal, tracing his journey from childhood to university. The Commission took serious note of the matter.

The OHRC has ordered a 13-point inquiry into how the names of the purported parents came to be recorded in Praveen’s documents and what remedial measures are needed to resolve the issue. The district collector has been directed to complete the inquiry within five days. The next hearing has been scheduled for September 1, 2026.

“This is a serious human rights concern and may not be an isolated case. The Women and Child Welfare Department should direct all childcare institutions to identify similar cases. As society moves increasingly towards digital records, discrepancies in educational and other personal documents can jeopardise a person’s future,” said human rights activist Biswapriya Kanungo.
